prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Classical effective potentials are indispensable for any large-scale atomistic simulations, and the relevance of simulation results crucially depends on the quality of the potentials used. For complex alloys like quasicrystals, however, realistic effective potentials are practically inexistent. We report here on our efforts to develop effective potentials especially for quasicrystalline alloy systems. We use the so-called force matching method, in which the potential parameters are adapted so as to optimally reproduce the forces and energies in a set of suitably chosen reference configurations. These reference data are calculated with ab-initio methods. As a first application, EAM potentials for decagonal Al-Ni-Co, icosahedral Ca-Cd, and both icosahedral and decagonal Mg-Zn quasicrystals have been constructed. The influence of the potential range and degree of specialisation on the accuracy and other properties is discussed and compared.

outputs.L1: Classical effective potentials are indispensable for large-scale atomistic simulations, and the relevance of the resulting predictions depends critically on the quality of the potentials employed. For complex alloys such as quasicrystals, however, realistic effective potentials are virtually nonexistent. Here, we report on our efforts to develop effective potentials specifically for quasicrystalline alloy systems. We employ the so-called force-matching method, in which the potential parameters are optimized to reproduce as accurately as possible the forces and energies of a suitably selected set of reference configurations. These reference data are calculated using *ab initio* methods. As an initial application, we have constructed embedded-atom method (EAM) potentials for decagonal Al-Ni-Co, icosahedral Ca-Cd, and both icosahedral and decagonal Mg-Zn quasicrystals. We discuss and compare the effects of potential range and degree of specialization on accuracy and other properties.
outputs.L2: Classical effective potentials are essential in large-scale atomistic modeling, and the reliability of simulation outcomes depends strongly on the accuracy of the chosen potentials. Yet realistic potentials are virtually unavailable for structurally complex alloys such as quasicrystals. Here, we describe our work toward creating effective potentials specifically for quasicrystalline alloy systems. Our approach employs force matching: potential parameters are optimized to reproduce as closely as possible the forces and energies of an appropriately selected collection of reference structures, with the reference values obtained from ab initio calculations. As initial applications, we have developed embedded-atom method (EAM) potentials for decagonal Al–Ni–Co, icosahedral Ca–Cd, and Mg–Zn quasicrystals in both icosahedral and decagonal forms. We also examine and compare how the interaction range and level of specialization affect accuracy and other characteristics of the potentials.
outputs.L3:
Classical effective potentials are indispensable for large-scale atomistic simulations because they make it possible to model systems containing many atoms over experimentally relevant time scales. However, the reliability of such simulations depends critically on the accuracy and transferability of the potentials employed. For structurally and chemically complex alloys, particularly quasicrystals, realistic effective potentials have remained largely unavailable.

To address this limitation, the researchers apply the force-matching method, in which potential parameters are optimized to reproduce atomic forces, total energies, and related quantities obtained from a carefully selected set of *ab initio* reference configurations. Using this approach, they developed embedded-atom method (EAM) potentials for several quasicrystalline systems: decagonal Al–Ni–Co, icosahedral Ca–Cd, and both icosahedral and decagonal Mg–Zn.

The study also systematically examines how the design of an effective potential influences its performance. In particular, it compares potentials with different interaction ranges and different degrees of specialization to determine how these choices affect fitting accuracy, transferability, and other relevant physical properties. The results provide insight into the compromises involved in constructing effective potentials for complex metallic alloys and offer practical guidance for future large-scale simulations of quasicrystals.
outputs.L4:
Realistic atomistic simulations of complex quasicrystalline alloys require reliable interatomic interactions, but suitable effective potentials are available for only a small number of these materials. The structural complexity of quasicrystals, their large characteristic length scales, and the presence of several chemical species make conventional potential construction particularly difficult. To address this problem, effective interactions were developed using the force-matching method. In this approach, the parameters of an embedded-atom-method potential are optimized so that the forces, total energies, and stresses predicted by the potential reproduce corresponding data obtained from first-principles calculations.

The fitting database was assembled from carefully selected reference configurations representing the relevant local environments in each alloy system. These configurations included crystalline approximants, distorted structures, and other atomic arrangements chosen to sample a broad range of bond lengths, coordinations, compositions, and thermodynamic conditions. Ab initio calculations supplied the target forces and energies, while numerical optimization was used to adjust the pair interactions, electron-density functions, and embedding terms of the effective potentials. Independent configurations not included in the fit were then used to assess transferability.

Using this procedure, successful potentials were constructed for several important quasicrystal-forming systems: decagonal Al-Ni-Co, icosahedral Ca-Cd, and both icosahedral and decagonal Mg-Zn. The resulting models reproduced the reference forces and energies with sufficient accuracy to permit large-scale molecular-dynamics and structural-relaxation studies that would be impractical with direct electronic-structure calculations. They also provided physically reasonable descriptions of the characteristic local coordination environments and energetic differences among competing structures.

Comparisons among alternative fits demonstrated that the form and range of the potential strongly influence its performance. Longer-ranged interactions can capture structural correlations extending beyond the nearest-neighbor shell and may therefore improve the description of complex quasicrystalline order. However, increasing the cutoff also raises computational cost and does not automatically guarantee better transferability. Conversely, shorter-ranged potentials are more efficient but may omit interactions needed to distinguish closely related structures or stabilize particular motifs.

The study also showed that highly specialized potentials can achieve excellent accuracy within the narrow class of structures represented in the fitting database, yet perform less reliably when applied to different compositions, phases, or thermodynamic conditions. More broadly fitted potentials may sacrifice some precision for a specific structure while providing a more balanced description across a wider range of environments. Potential quality therefore cannot be judged solely by the fitting error: structural stability, elastic response, transferability, computational efficiency, and the intended application must all be considered.

Overall, the results establish force matching to ab initio data as a practical route for constructing effective potentials for complex quasicrystalline alloys. The work provides usable models for several representative decagonal and icosahedral systems while clarifying the trade-offs associated with interaction range and degree of specialization. These potentials make it possible to investigate larger systems and longer timescales, opening the way to simulations of structural stability, defects, diffusion, phason-related processes, and finite-temperature behavior in quasicrystals and their approximants.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an abstract for a research paper on developing classical effective potentials for quasicrystalline alloys using ab initio force matching.
counterfactuals.output: We present a framework for developing classical effective interatomic potentials for quasicrystalline alloys using force matching to an ab initio reference database. Density-functional-theory calculations are performed for periodic approximants, competing crystalline phases, and thermally sampled configurations chosen to represent the diverse local environments characteristic of quasiperiodic structures. The resulting energies, atomic forces, and stresses are used to parameterize a computationally efficient potential with physically motivated pairwise and many-body contributions. Validation against configurations excluded from fitting demonstrates the model’s ability to reproduce ab initio structural energetics, force distributions, elastic response, and defect-related rearrangements across relevant compositions and temperatures. Particular attention is given to the transferability of the potential between approximants and to its description of phason-associated atomic motion and local chemical ordering. The resulting model enables molecular-dynamics simulations at length and time scales inaccessible to first-principles methods while retaining near-ab initio accuracy in the sampled configuration space. This approach provides a systematic route for investigating the thermodynamic stability, structural transformations, defect dynamics, and finite-temperature behavior of complex quasicrystalline alloys.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize efforts to construct EAM potentials for decagonal Al-Ni-Co, icosahedral Ca-Cd, and icosahedral and decagonal Mg-Zn quasicrystals, including the methodology and factors affecting accuracy.
counterfactuals.output:
Efforts to model these quasicrystals have generally used **ab-initio force matching** to construct multicomponent embedded-atom-method (EAM) potentials. The EAM energy is written as

\[
E=\frac12\sum_{i\ne j}\phi_{\alpha_i\alpha_j}(r_{ij})
+\sum_i F_{\alpha_i}\!\left(\sum_{j\ne i}\rho_{\alpha_j}(r_{ij})\right),
\]

with pair interactions \(\phi\), elemental electron-density contributions \(\rho\), and embedding functions \(F\). These functions are usually represented by splines and optimized—often with the *potfit* approach—against density-functional-theory forces, energies, and stresses for small periodic approximants, distorted structures, liquids, and competing crystalline phases.

### Decagonal Al–Ni–Co
Al–Ni–Co was an early and difficult target. Force-matched potentials were developed to permit simulations much larger than direct DFT calculations, including structural relaxation and annealing of decagonal approximants. Pair-potential fits captured some medium-range, oscillatory interactions, while EAM terms were introduced to account for environmental dependence. Accuracy remained limited because:

- Ni and Co have partially filled \(d\) states and chemically specific, partly directional bonding;
- Al–transition-metal and transition-metal–transition-metal interactions must distinguish very similar local environments;
- small energy differences control chemical ordering and phason configurations;
- approximant-based databases do not necessarily sample all environments present in a large decagonal phase.

Thus, such potentials can reproduce many DFT forces and broad structural motifs but are less reliable for subtle site occupations, defect energies, and relative stability between nearly degenerate structures.

### Icosahedral Ca–Cd
Ca–Cd, including CaCd\(_6\)-type approximants and the icosahedral phase, is more amenable to an EAM description because its bonding is comparatively metallic and less strongly directional. DFT force-matched EAM potentials have been used to study Tsai-type cluster packing, relaxation, and orientational behavior of inner Cd clusters. Their quality depends strongly on including:

- both quasicrystal approximants and competing Ca–Cd crystals;
- different orientations and distortions of the central clusters;
- a sufficiently wide range of volumes and local densities.

Fits restricted to equilibrium approximants may reproduce their structure well but perform poorly for cluster reorientation, defects, high-temperature disorder, or structures with densities outside the fitted range.

### Icosahedral and decagonal Mg–Zn
Mg–Zn EAM potentials have been fitted with the aim of describing both icosahedral and decagonal structures, as well as related Frank–Kasper and approximant phases. A joint database is important because a potential fitted only to one structural family may stabilize it artificially and fail for the other. These potentials generally reproduce metallic coordination and bulk structural trends reasonably well, but the relative energies of competing Mg–Zn phases are extremely small. Consequently, phase selection, site occupancy, and quasicrystal-versus-approximant stability are more demanding tests than the force-fitting error alone.

### Main factors controlling accuracy
Across all three systems, accuracy is governed primarily by:

1. **Training-set coverage**—compositions, temperatures, volumes, distortions, defects, liquids, approximants, and competing phases must all be represented.
2. **Quality of the DFT reference data**, including exchange-correlation treatment, convergence, and treatment of transition-metal electronic structure.
3. **Functional flexibility and cutoffs**—short cutoffs or overly smooth spline forms can miss Friedel-like oscillations and medium-range interactions important in quasicrystals.
4. **Balance of fitting targets**—forces dominate numerically, but energies and stresses are essential for correct phase stability and elastic behavior.
5. **Transferability**—a low force error within the fitting database does not guarantee correct behavior for new compositions, phason defects, surfaces, or high-temperature states.
6. **Intrinsic EAM limitations**—standard EAM represents environment dependence through a scalar local density and therefore cannot fully capture directional or chemically complex bonding, particularly in Al–Ni–Co.
7. **Non-uniqueness of EAM functions**—gauge freedoms and correlations among pair, density, and embedding terms require regularization and validation against properties not included in the fit.

Overall, force-matched EAM models made atomistic simulations of large quasicrystal approximants practical and often reproduced local structure and dynamics well. Their weakest point is usually not the fitted forces themselves, but the very small energetic differences governing chemical order, phason states, and competition among quasicrystalline and crystalline phases.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a concise scientific conference abstract explaining why realistic interatomic potentials are needed for large-scale quasicrystal simulations and how force matching can be used to create them.
counterfactuals.output:
**Force-Matched Interatomic Potentials for Large-Scale Quasicrystal Simulations**

Quasicrystals exhibit complex, aperiodic atomic order, large structural motifs, and collective phenomena such as phason rearrangements, defect motion, and long-range strain relaxation. Simulating these processes requires systems and timescales far beyond the reach of density-functional theory. Conventional empirical potentials are computationally efficient but often fail to reproduce the diverse local environments and competing interactions that stabilize quasicrystalline phases. Realistic, transferable interatomic potentials are therefore essential for connecting quantum-mechanical accuracy with large-scale molecular dynamics.

Force matching provides a systematic route to constructing such potentials. A representative database of quasicrystal approximants, competing crystalline phases, defects, strained structures, and finite-temperature configurations is first evaluated using first-principles calculations. Potential parameters are then optimized to reproduce the resulting atomic forces, energies, and stresses. Careful sampling and independent validation ensure accuracy across relevant structural and thermodynamic conditions. The resulting force-matched potentials enable simulations of quasicrystal stability, growth, phason dynamics, mechanical response, and defect evolution at experimentally meaningful length and time scales.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Describe a study in which potential parameters are fitted to ab initio forces and energies from selected reference configurations, with applications to several complex alloy systems.
counterfactuals.output:
The study used a **force-matching approach** to construct effective interatomic potentials for complex metallic alloys. A database of representative configurations—crystals, approximants, distorted structures, liquids, and thermally generated snapshots—was first calculated with density-functional theory. The potential parameters were then optimized by minimizing a weighted least-squares objective containing:

- differences between model and **ab initio atomic forces**,
- differences in total or relative **energies**, and, where available,
- stress information and additional constraints needed for stability.

Because each configuration supplies three force components per atom, the method provides much more fitting information than an energy-only database. The resulting potentials were validated on structures not included in the fit and then used in molecular-dynamics or structural-relaxation calculations beyond the size and time scales accessible to direct DFT.

Applications included complex and quasicrystal-related alloy systems such as **decagonal Al–Ni–Co**, **icosahedral Ca–Cd**, and **Mg–Zn** alloys. The work showed that carefully selected reference configurations and simultaneous force–energy fitting can produce computationally efficient potentials capable of reproducing structural energetics, atomic relaxations, and finite-temperature behavior in chemically and structurally complicated alloys.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a journal-style abstract titled “Effective Potentials for Quasicrystalline Alloys,” mentioning EAM construction, force matching, potential range, degree of specialization, and comparative accuracy.
counterfactuals.output:
# Effective Potentials for Quasicrystalline Alloys

We present a systematic framework for developing effective interatomic potentials for quasicrystalline alloys, where complex local environments and aperiodic order challenge conventional parameterizations. Embedded-atom method (EAM) potentials are constructed from reference first-principles data and optimized through force matching to energies, atomic forces, and stresses sampled across crystalline approximants, competing phases, defects, and thermally disordered configurations. We examine how the potential range influences structural stability and transferability, finding that sufficiently extended interactions are required to distinguish closely related coordination environments. We also assess the degree of specialization needed to reproduce quasicrystal-specific motifs without compromising applicability to periodic phases and off-stoichiometric structures. Comparative tests against standard EAM models, simpler pair potentials, and density-functional calculations show that specialized force-matched potentials achieve improved accuracy for energies, forces, elastic response, and phase ordering, while retaining computational efficiency. These results clarify the balance among interaction range, model flexibility, specialization, and predictive accuracy in atomistic simulations of quasicrystalline alloys.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
